pages.x: In the rich, sunny south of France, in Languedoc, many people followed the Cathars, Good Men and Good Women who taught that the world was the work of an evil power, and lived lives of poverty and fasting. The Church called them heretics, and the lords of the south, above all the count of Toulouse, would not root them out.

In 1208 a papal legate was murdered, and Pope Innocent III blamed Count Raymond VI of Toulouse. He called a crusade against the heretics, promising the knights who joined it the same forgiveness of sins as a crusade to the Holy Land, and the heretics' lands as well.

In July 1209 the crusaders stormed Béziers and massacred its people, Catholics and Cathars alike, many in the churches where they had taken refuge. A monk later wrote that the pope's legate, asked how to tell them apart, answered, "Kill them all. God will know his own," though he may never have said it.

Carcassonne surrendered weeks later, and its lands were given to a hard northern baron, Simon de Montfort. He took the Cathar strongholds one by one, and at Minerve and Lavaur burned hundreds of Cathars alive. At Bram he had a hundred prisoners blinded, leaving one man a single eye to lead the rest.

King Peter II of Aragon, overlord of many southern lords and a hero of the wars against the Moors in Spain, crossed the Pyrenees to protect his vassals. At Muret in September 1213, Montfort's much smaller force charged and killed him, and the southern army fled.

In 1217 Toulouse rose again for its count, and Montfort laid siege to it. On 25 June 1218 a stone from a catapult on the walls, worked, the song of the crusade says, by the women and girls of the city, struck him on the head and killed him.

Simon's son could not hold his father's conquests, and in 1224 he handed his rights to the king of France. In 1226 King Louis VIII led a royal army south, and most towns submitted. By the Treaty of Paris in 1229 the count of Toulouse gave up much of his land, and his heiress was married to the new king's brother.

To finish the Cathars off, the Church set up the Inquisition. In 1244 their last great stronghold, the mountain castle of Montségur, fell after a siege of ten months, and more than two hundred Cathars who would not give up their faith were burned together on a great pyre below it.
pages.of: Cathars burned at Montségur in one day

pages.x: The crusade brought the south into the kingdom of France, and the Inquisition stamped out the Cathars within a century. The south's own language, Occitan, and the culture of its troubadours slowly faded, and the ruined Cathar castles on their crags still haunt the landscape.
